question: Which of the following statements is/are characteristic of the process of metamorphism?

options.a: Under isochemical conditions the bulk chemistry of the rock remains essentially unchanged (except H2O/CO2)
options.b: There is no large-scale silicate liquid (magma) present at any given time
options.c: There is no fixed order of crystallization as seen in igneous melts; recrystallization occurs essentially in the solid state

notes: Metamorphism is essentially an isochemical solid-state recrystallization of pre-existing rocks under changing P-T-fluid conditions, without large-scale melting.

question: The primary fundamental type of chemical reaction involved in prograde metamorphism is:
notes: Prograde metamorphism is dominated by endothermic devolatilization reactions wherein hydrous or carbonate solid phases break down into denser anhydrous solids plus a liberated vapor phase (H2O or CO2).

question: Thermal or contact metamorphism in an aureole surrounding an igneous pluton is characteristically governed by:

options.a: High temperature, low pressure, low deviatoric strain, and variable fluid pressure
options.b: High temperature, high pressure, low strain, and variable fluid pressure
options.c: High temperature, low pressure, variable strain, and high fluid pressure
options.d: High temperature, high pressure, high strain, and high fluid pressure

notes: Contact metamorphism occurs in shallow crustal regimes adjacent to magma intrusions, characterized by elevated temperature under low lithostatic pressure and minimal directed shear strain.

question: Which of the following metamorphic rocks has NOT resulted due to contact metamorphism?
notes: Augen gneisses form through high-grade dynamothermal regional metamorphism accompanied by intense ductile shear strain, unlike static contact spotted slates, hornfelses, and skarns.

question: Hornfelses developed in the inner contact aureole generally possess a:

options.c: Combination of porphyroblastic (andalusite/cordierite) and fine-grained granoblastic matrix fabric

notes: Hornfelses typically exhibit a fine-grained granoblastic (saccharoidal) interlocking matrix often punctuated by unoriented porphyroblasts of cordierite, andalusite, or biotite.

question: Thermal contact metamorphism of a dolomitic limestone containing small amounts of siliceous (quartz) impurity leads to the formation of:
notes: At high temperatures, dolomite reacts with quartz via the decarbonation reaction: 2 Dolomite + Quartz -> Forsterite + 2 Calcite + 2 CO2, producing forsterite marble.

question: Metamorphism involving substantial, pervasive allochemical addition or removal of chemical components by circulating hydrothermal fluids is termed:
notes: Metasomatism is an allochemical metamorphic process driven by fluid infiltration that drastically alters the bulk chemical composition of the rock.

question: Metamorphism involving the combined effect of high uniform lithostatic pressure and high heat at great crustal depths is described as:
notes: In Grubenmann's classic scheme, plutonic metamorphism operates in the deep katazone where intense hydrostatic confining pressure and high geothermal temperatures produce granoblastic fabrics with minimal foliation.

question: The development of tectonites (deformed rocks with preferred mineral lattice or shape orientation) is widespread in:
notes: Dynamothermal (orogenic) regional metamorphism couples deviatoric shear strain with elevated temperatures, driving pervasive fabric development in S-, L-, and L-S tectonites.

question: Which of the following metamorphic types is matched correctly with its dominant physical agent?

options.b: Contact metamorphism — High directed stress predominant
options.c: Kinetic (dynamic) metamorphism — Directed shear pressure predominant
options.d: Pneumatolysis — Changes due to dry solid-state heating alone

notes: Kinetic (dynamic or cataclastic) metamorphism is driven primarily by intense directed differential stress along fault and shear zones, producing cataclasites and mylonites.

question: Choose the scientifically correct physical statement regarding pressure in metamorphic geology:

options.a: Uniform (hydrostatic/lithostatic) pressure acts equally in all directions on both liquids and solids
options.b: Directed pressure causes a change in volume alone without shape distortion
options.c: Uniform pressure leads to a change of surface area without volume compaction
options.d: All of the above are correct

notes: Uniform lithostatic pressure acts isotropically (equal magnitude in all spatial directions) on solid rock and pore fluid alike, reducing volume without changing shape.

question: When uniform confining or hydrostatic pressure acts on a solid rock body during burial, its:

options.a: Volume decreases and specific gravity decreases
options.b: Volume increases and specific gravity increases
options.c: Volume decreases but specific gravity (density) increases
options.d: Volume increases but specific gravity decreases

notes: Confining pressure compresses mineral lattices and collapses pore spaces, decreasing molar volume and consequently increasing specific gravity and density.

question: Which of the following physical and crystallographic effects take place when a rock body is subjected to directed differential pressure? (i) Dilation, (ii) Distortion, (iii) Formation of inequidimensional grains, (iv) Growth of grains perpendicular to the direction of principal stress, (v) Increased mineral solubility at points of greatest stress (Riecke's principle). The correct combination is:
notes: Directed differential stress causes shape distortion, aligns inequidimensional grains, promotes growth perpendicular to maximum compression, and drives Riecke's dissolution at high-stress contacts.

question: Oriented platy/prismatic mineral grains producing a strongly foliated (schistose) rock appearance are characteristic of metamorphic rocks belonging to the:
notes: In the Grubenmann-Niggli depth classification, the Mesozone is characterized by moderate temperatures and pronounced directed stress, producing classic mica schists and amphibolites.

question: Which of the following metamorphic rocks are completely unfoliated (granulose / hornfelsic)?
notes: Hornfelses, quartzites, and marbles are non-foliated granulose rocks lacking planar alignment of phyllosilicates, in sharp contrast to slates, phyllites, and schists.

question: Minerals whose fields of thermodynamic stability on a P-T diagram are extended or favored by the introduction of non-hydrostatic differential stress are termed:
notes: Alfred Harker (1932) defined 'stress minerals' (e.g., kyanite, staurolite, chloritoid, almandine) as phases whose crystallization is favored in dynamic orogenic environments with high shear stress.

question: Stress minerals are crystallographically characterized by: (i) High packing index of crystal lattice, (ii) Low molar volume, (iii) High density, (iv) Equidimensional habit. Which statements are correct?
notes: Stress minerals possess closely packed atomic structures (high packing index), exceptionally low molar volumes, and high specific gravities; they are commonly inequidimensional.

question: Among the three Al2SiO5 polymorphs, which mineral is a classic stress mineral favored by high pressure and shear stress?
notes: Kyanite has the highest density (3.53-3.65 g/cm3) and smallest molar volume among the Al2SiO5 polymorphs, making it the diagnostic high-pressure stress mineral.

question: Stress minerals (such as chloritoid and staurolite) are generally absent in rocks belonging to the:

options.c: Katazone (very high T, hydrostatic P, low shear stress)

notes: In the deepest Katazone, intense thermal energy and high confining pressure eliminate directed differential stress, so stress minerals give way to anhydrous granoblastic phases.

question: Metamorphic minerals that develop their own euhedral crystal faces in spite of the resistance of the surrounding solid crystalline medium are described as:
notes: Idioblastic minerals develop well-defined crystal boundaries by virtue of high form energy (crystalloblastic strength), whereas xenoblastic minerals are bounded by irregular growth surfaces.

question: Which of the following mineral sequences is arranged in the correct order of decreasing idioblastic form energy (Becke's Crystalloblastic Series)?
notes: In Becke's Crystalloblastic Series, minerals with high form energy (sphene, rutile, garnet, staurolite) crystallize idioblastically against phyllosilicates, carbonates, and quartz/feldspar.

question: In regional metamorphic rocks of the greenschist to amphibolite facies, the most commonly occurring potash feldspar is microcline and NOT orthoclase because:

options.d: Directed differential stress and moderate temperatures promote lattice ordering from monoclinic orthoclase into triclinic microcline

notes: Directed shear stress accelerates the kinetic ordering of Al-Si distributions in K-feldspar, converting monoclinic orthoclase into the ordered triclinic polymorph, microcline.

question: The presence of large, well-formed metamorphic crystals (porphyroblasts) enclosed within a fine-grained recrystallized groundmass is described as a:
notes: Porphyroblastic texture consists of large metamorphic crystals (e.g., garnet, staurolite, andalusite) grown in the solid state within a finer-grained matrix, differing from igneous porphyritic textures.

question: Large metamorphic porphyroblasts that contain numerous unoriented or oriented micro-inclusions of quartz, graphite, or mica are termed:
notes: Poikiloblastic (sieve) texture develops when rapidly growing porphyroblasts engulf surrounding matrix grains that cannot be expelled from the growing crystal lattice.

question: Metamorphic textures characterized by the preferred planar parallel alignment of platy, micaceous, or flaky minerals (biotite, muscovite, chlorite) are described as:
notes: Lepidoblastic texture (from Greek lepis, scale) describes rocks whose foliation is defined by parallel-aligned flaky or lamellar phyllosilicates, as in schists.

question: Metamorphic textures characterized by the parallel or subparallel alignment of prismatic, acicular, or needle-like minerals (amphiboles, sillimanite) are described as:
notes: Nematoblastic texture (from Greek nema, thread) is defined by the preferred linear alignment of prismatic or needle-like crystals, typical of amphibolites.

question: An equigranular metamorphic texture composed of interlocking, polygonal or anhedral quartz, feldspar, or calcite grains meeting at ~120° triple junctions is described as:
notes: Granoblastic texture consists of equigranular, xenoblastic to subhedral grains forming a mosaic, characteristic of quartzites, marbles, and granulites.

question: A random, interlocking criss-cross arrangement of prismatic or platy minerals (e.g., biotite, anthophyllite) lacking any preferred orientation is termed:
notes: Decussate texture develops under thermally dominated, low-strain contact or regional conditions where crystals nucleate and grow in random, unoriented directions to minimize interfacial free energy.

question: The metamorphic texture in which large, rounded to augen-shaped feldspar or quartz porphyroclasts are enclosed within a finely crushed, granulated matrix is termed:
notes: Mortar texture forms by intense brittle-ductile mechanical crushing along shear zones, wherein grain boundaries are ground into fine pulverized matrix surrounding uncrushed porphyroclast cores.

question: Contorted, microfolded, or sigmoidal trails of inclusion trains preserved inside a poikiloblastic garnet or staurolite host represent a/an:
notes: Helicitic structures preserve internal inclusion trails (Si) reflecting pre-existing folds or syn-tectonic crystal rotation relative to the external foliation (Se).

question: 'Maculose' structure (spotted or nodular fabric) is characteristically developed during low-grade contact metamorphism of:
notes: Spotted slates (maculose rocks) form in the outer aureole of contact zones where incipient thermal recrystallization produces dark spots/nodules of cordierite or carbonaceous matter in pelites.

question: If a metamorphic foliated structure is dominated exclusively by elongated prismatic minerals like hornblende or sillimanite, it is classified as:
notes: Nematoblastic fabric designates metamorphic lineations and foliations constructed primarily by subparallel prismatic inosilicates.

question: The 'Muth Quartzites' of Devonian age in the Himalayas characteristically exhibit which distinctive metamorphic/sedimentary texture under microscopy?

options.d: Granulose / mosaic texture with syntaxial quartz overgrowths

notes: The Muth Quartzite exhibits a supermature granulose mosaic texture composed of well-rounded detrital quartz clasts cemented by optical-continuous syntaxial quartz overgrowths.

question: Metamorphic facies (Pentti Eskola, 1915, 1920) are scientifically defined by:

options.a: Conditions of temperature and pressure alone
options.b: A single dominant lithological rock type
options.c: Critical equilibrium mineral assemblages that recur in rocks of a given bulk chemical composition

notes: A metamorphic facies comprises all rocks that have reached chemical equilibrium under similar P-T conditions, defined rigorously by critical diagnostic mineral assemblages for specific rock chemistries.

question: Which of the following metamorphic facies is characterized by the absolute MAXIMUM temperatures and MINIMUM confining pressures in Earth's crust?
notes: The sanidinite facies represents extreme pyrometamorphism (volcanic xenoliths or direct basalt contact) operating at temperatures >800-1000°C under near-atmospheric to very low lithostatic pressure.

question: Which metamorphic facies represents the gradual thermodynamic transition between diagenesis (burial) and regional metamorphism?
notes: D.S. Coombs (1954) defined the zeolite facies (laumontite, wairakite, heulandite) to bridge the low-temperature gap (100-250°C) between sedimentary diagenesis and greenschist facies metamorphism.

question: The most voluminous and widespread of all regional metamorphic rocks in continental collision orogens belong to which facies?
notes: The amphibolite facies forms the dominant crystalline basement of continental orogens and Precambrian shields, characterized by hornblende + plagioclase in basic rocks and garnet + staurolite + kyanite in pelites.

question: Which of the following metamorphic rocks are formed under abnormally LOW geothermal gradients (high P, low T) characteristic of subduction zones?
notes: Blueschists develop exclusively along cold subducting oceanic slab interfaces where rapid tectonic burial drives pressures to >6-12 kbar while temperatures remain depressed below 200-400°C.

question: The Garnet-Sillimanite Schists and Gneisses of the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt of India, universally known as 'Khondalites', belong to which metamorphic facies?
notes: Khondalites are restitic metapelitic granulites containing garnet + sillimanite + quartz + K-feldspar ± graphite, formed under ultra-high-temperature granulite facies conditions (>800°C, ~7-9 kbar).

question: The calc-silicate mineral assemblage Larnite + Merwinite + Spurrite is uniquely diagnostic of which extreme metamorphic facies?
notes: Larnite (beta-Ca2SiO4), spurrite, and merwinite crystallize at ultra-high contact temperatures (>900°C) and low pressures in siliceous carbonate xenoliths within the sanidinite facies.

question: Match the metamorphic facies with its critical diagnostic index mineral: (A) Zeolite facies -> 3. Laumontite; (B) Sanidinite facies -> 4. Sanidine; (C) Blueschist facies -> 1. Lawsonite; (D) Greenschist facies -> 2. Chlorite. The correct match is:
notes: Laumontite diagnoses zeolite facies; sanidine diagnoses sanidinite facies; lawsonite/glaucophane diagnoses blueschist facies; chlorite/actinolite diagnoses greenschist facies.

question: Which sodic amphibole is uniquely diagnostic of high-pressure, low-temperature blueschist facies metamorphism?
notes: Glaucophane is a blue sodic amphibole whose stability is restricted to low geothermal gradients (<10°C/km) and high lithostatic pressures (>6-10 kbar) in subduction complexes.

question: Hydrous or hydroxyl-bearing silicate minerals (micas, amphiboles) are essentially ABSENT in the anhydrous rocks of which metamorphic facies?
notes: Under granulite and eclogite facies conditions, complete prograde dehydration drives off all hydroxyl groups, yielding dry anhydrous assemblages of pyroxenes, garnets, plagioclase, and quartz.

question: In metamorphosed siliceous carbonate rocks, which of the following represents the LEAST silicic (most silica-depleted / silica-undersaturated) mineral assemblage?
notes: Periclase (MgO) forms by the complete decarbonation of dolomite (Dolomite -> Calcite + Periclase + CO2) only when silica is completely exhausted, representing maximum silica undersaturation.

question: Which polymorphic mineral group serves as the quintessential 'geological barometer and thermometer' across metamorphic petrology?
notes: The Al2SiO5 polymorphs share identical chemistry and invariant triple point (~500°C, 3.8 kbar; Holdaway, 1971), making their coexistence the universal P-T calibration standard.

question: In subduction-accretion complexes of the blueschist facies terranes, eclogites characteristically occur as:

options.b: Horizontal stratiform sheets hundreds of km wide
options.d: Isolated lenticular boudins and tectonic blocks entrained within serpentinite shear zones

notes: Dense high-pressure eclogites (omphacite + pyrope) occur as dense tectonic lenses, boudins, and pods exhumed within blueschist or serpentinite subduction mélanges.

question: Omphacite, the diagnostic jadeite-bearing sodic clinopyroxene of eclogites, is chemically characterized by:

options.a: High Na2O and Al2O3, with very low K2O

notes: Omphacite is a solid solution of diopside/hedenbergite with jadeite [NaAlSi2O6], characterized by high sodium and octahedral aluminum stabilized by high subduction pressures.

question: In terms of whole-rock bulk chemical composition, bimineralic eclogites (omphacite + pyrope-almandine garnet) are isochemical equivalents of:
notes: Eclogite is the high-pressure metamorphic equivalent of basalt or gabbro: under pressures >12-15 kbar, plagioclase breaks down completely into omphacite + garnet + quartz.

question: With a drop in temperature and influx of hydrous pore fluids, rocks belonging to the granulite facies undergo retrograde metamorphism into amphibolite facies via which sequence?

options.a: Pyroxene-granulite facies -> Hornblende-granulite facies -> Amphibolite facies
options.b: Hornblende-granulite facies -> Pyroxene-granulite facies -> Amphibolite facies
options.c: Granulite facies -> Eclogite facies -> Amphibolite facies
options.d: Granulite facies -> Blueschist facies -> Amphibolite facies

notes: Retrograde hydration of dry pyroxene-granulites produces hornblende-bearing granulite intermediates before completely recrystallizing into hydrous amphibolites (hornblende + plagioclase).

question: Which of the following field and petrographic factors provide conclusive proof for an igneous or magmatic origin of charnockitic suites?

options.a: Presence of mesoperthite, prevalence of rare Albite-Ala twins, accessory pyrrhotite, and cross-cutting intrusive apophyses into country rocks
options.d: Presence of diagnostic bedding and ripple marks

notes: High-temperature mesoperthitic alkali feldspar, Albite-Ala twinning, orthopyroxene, and intrusive apophyses demonstrate that many charnockites crystallized from dry, CO2-rich deep crustal magmas.

question: If a metamorphic foliated structure is dominated exclusively by elongated prismatic minerals like hornblende or sillimanite, it is classified as:
notes: Nematoblastic texture designates metamorphic rocks whose fabric is defined by the parallel or subparallel alignment of prismatic or acicular minerals.

question: The 'Muth Quartzites' of Devonian age in the Himalayas characteristically exhibit which distinctive metamorphic/sedimentary texture under microscopy?

options.b: Cataclastic texture / fractured quartz grains with syntaxial rims

notes: In deformed Himalayan zones, the Muth Quartzite exhibits brittle cataclastic fracturing, undulatory extinction, and mortar textures along grain boundaries.

question: Metamorphic facies (Pentti Eskola, 1915, 1920) are scientifically defined by:

options.a: Conditions of temperature and pressure alone
options.c: Peculiar textures and structures of the rock types
options.d: Critical equilibrium mineral assemblages that recur in rocks of a given bulk chemical composition

notes: A metamorphic facies is defined by critical equilibrium mineral assemblages that reflect specific ranges of pressure and temperature for specific protolith chemistries.

question: In the progressive regional metamorphic transition from Shale to Gneiss (Shale -> Slate -> Phyllite -> Schist -> Gneiss), the average grain size of the rock:

options.c: Increases progressively due to solid-state grain growth and recrystallization

notes: Prograde metamorphism drives grain coarsening: sub-micron clay in shales recrystallizes into microcrystalline phyllosilicates in slates, coarse mica flakes in schists, and coarse megascopic bands in gneisses.

question: A Gneiss is petrologically distinguished from a Schist primarily by:

options.a: Alternating bands of granular minerals (quartz, feldspar) and flaky/prismatic minerals (biotite, hornblende)

notes: Gneisses exhibit gneissic compositional banding where granular felsic domains (quartz and feldspar) alternate with dark mafic/lepidoblastic foliae (biotite, amphibole).

question: A fine-grained pelitic metamorphic rock intermediate between slate and schist, possessing a silky lustrous cleavage sheen caused by minute sericite and chlorite flakes, is termed a:
notes: Phyllite exhibits a characteristic silky, lustrous sheen on cleavage surfaces resulting from the growth of microscopic white mica (sericite) and chlorite.

question: Slaty cleavage in low-grade metamorphic rocks (slates) develops primarily due to:

options.a: Pervasive mechanical rotation and recrystallization of minute platy clay minerals and sericite perpendicular to maximum compression

notes: Slaty cleavage forms during tectonic shortening by ductile deformation, mechanical rotation, and pressure-solution alignment of phyllosilicates perpendicular to the principal shortening axis.

question: A secondary cleavage produced by the micro-folding (crenulation) of a pre-existing slaty cleavage or schistosity is described as:
notes: Strain-slip (crenulation) cleavage superimposes on an earlier foliation, producing micro-crenulations whose limbs thin and recrystallize into a new secondary planar cleavage.

question: Which of the following planar structures in metamorphic geology is a primary rock cleavage independent of mineral alignment, consisting of closely spaced parallel shear fractures?
notes: Fracture cleavage consists of true mechanical fractures or joints spaced at narrow regular intervals, developing independently of internal mineral lattice alignment.

question: Metamorphic rocks produced purely by mechanical crushing, grinding, and cataclastic granulation along fault zones without significant chemical reconstitution are termed:
notes: Cataclasites are non-foliated fault rocks formed in the brittle upper crust by mechanical crushing, grain fracturing, and comminution without neocrystallization.

question: A cohesive, strongly foliated fault rock displaying intense ductile grain-size reduction, dynamic recrystallization, and ribbony quartz ribbons is scientifically classified as a:
notes: Charles Lapworth (1885) defined mylonites as cohesive, foliated rocks produced by intense crystal-plastic strain and dynamic recrystallization in ductile shear zones.

question: Dark, glassy to crypto-crystalline veinlets formed by extreme frictional melting of rock along high-velocity seismic fault slip planes are termed:
notes: Pseudotachylytes are fossil earthquake slip zones where rapid coseismic friction melts wall-rock, quenching into black glassy veinlets with injection offshoots.

question: A deformed rock in which lens-shaped, sheared lenticles of parent rock ('flasers') are wrapped around by fine-grained granulated or micaceous shear bands is termed a:
notes: Flaser rocks exhibit lenticular domains (flasers) of preserved parent rock wrapped by anastomosing ribbons of sheared and dynamically recrystallized matrix.

question: Relict metamorphic textures that preserve the original blasto-igneous or blasto-sedimentary fabrics are collectively designated as:
notes: Palimpsest (blastic) textures preserve recognizable features of the pre-metamorphic protolith (e.g., blastoporphyritic, blasto-ophitic, blasto-psephitic).

question: A metamorphic rock that preserves relict igneous phenocrysts embedded within a recrystallized groundmass is described as:
notes: Blastoporphyritic texture denotes metamorphic rocks where original igneous phenocrysts have survived recrystallization of the fine groundmass.

question: A relict texture in which metamorphic plagioclase laths are partially enclosed within relict or pseudomorphed pyroxenes, inherited from an original doleritic protolith, is termed:
notes: Blasto-ophitic texture preserves the interlocking lath-and-pyroxene geometry of an igneous diabase or gabbro in meta-dolerites and ortho-amphibolites.

question: Relicts of original sedimentary bedding, phenocrysts, or amygdules that persist through low- to medium-grade metamorphism are termed:
notes: Palimpsest features represent pre-existing textures that survived metamorphic overprinting, akin to an ancient parchment scraped and reused.

question: Metamorphic crystals that have grown entirely in the solid state but have developed perfect, planar, euhedral geometric crystal boundaries are described as:
notes: Idioblastic (automorphic) crystals exhibit sharp, planar crystal faces formed during solid-state growth by minerals with exceptionally high form energy (garnet, tourmaline, rutile).

question: Metamorphic crystals that lack any regular crystal faces and are bounded by irregular, interlocking, or rounded margins are described as:
notes: Xenoblastic crystals lack crystallographic crystal faces due to mutual interference during solid-state growth or low form energy (quartz, calcite, alkali feldspar).

question: 'Enderbites' in the high-grade granulite facies charnockitic suites are petrologically defined as:

options.a: Tonalitic charnockites composed essentially of quartz, plagioclase (antiperthite), and hypersthene, with minimal K-feldspar

notes: Enderbites are members of the charnockite suite dominated by plagioclase (antiperthitic oligoclase-andesine), quartz, and hypersthene, with little to no K-feldspar (charnockitic tonalite).

question: Gneissic rocks that have originated from the high-grade metamorphism of sedimentary protoliths (e.g., arkoses, graywackes, pelites) are described as:
notes: Paragneisses derive from sedimentary protoliths (exhibiting high Al2O3, normative corundum, high K/Na), while orthogneisses derive from igneous granites/diorites.

question: Which of the following geochemical criteria can be reliably used to establish a SEDIMENTARY protolith for high-grade paragneisses? (i) Excess of alumina (normative corundum > 1%), (ii) Very high total silica content (>75%) coupled with high K2O > Na2O, (iii) Rounded detrital zircon cores with overgrowths. The correct combination is:

options.d: All of the above (i, ii, and iii)

notes: High Al2O3/alkali ratios (normative corundum), high K/Na, high SiO2, and detrital zircon morphologies collectively confirm a sedimentary origin for paragneisses.

question: In V.M. Goldschmidt's Mineralogical Phase Rule ($P \le C$), the thermodynamic conditions for stable mineral equilibrium in metamorphic rocks are met when:

options.c: Variance F >= 2 (divariant equilibrium P = C over a finite range of P and T)

notes: Because metamorphic assemblages persist across broad geographical zones (finite ranges of P and T), F must be at least 2, requiring that the number of phases P cannot exceed the number of components C ($P \le C$).

question: A 'Buchite' is scientifically classified as a/an:

options.a: Partially fused, vitrified pyrometamorphic hornfelsic rock occurring as xenoliths in basaltic magmas
options.b: Fine-grained flinty rock formed by extreme cataclastic dislocation
options.c: Rock formed by mechanical disintegration of graywackes

notes: Buchites are high-temperature pyrometamorphic rocks wherein pelitic or psammitic xenoliths undergo partial melting (fritting) against basaltic melts, producing abundant glass (mullite, cordierite, glass).

question: Relict metamorphic textures inherited from fine-grained argillaceous sedimentary rocks (shales) are described as:
notes: Blasto-pelitic textures preserve the fine-grained laminated structure of argillaceous clayrocks and shales.

question: Relicts of original sedimentary or igneous minerals and textures preserved in metamorphic rocks are termed:
notes: Palimpsest (relict) textures represent original pre-metamorphic mineral and textural remnants that survived recrystallization.

question: When idioblastic crystals of garnet or staurolite are embedded within a finer-grained recrystallized groundmass, the resulting texture is termed:
notes: Porphyroblastic texture describes large metamorphic crystals (porphyroblasts) grown in a solid groundmass, differing from relict blastoporphyritic igneous crystals.

question: Any retrograde reversal of metamorphism which produces lower-grade mineral assemblages from higher-grade rocks is termed:
notes: Diaphthoresis (retrograde metamorphism) involves the hydration and adjustment of high-grade rocks to lower-grade P-T conditions, often along shear zones.

question: The retrograde hydration and pseudomorphic alteration of cordierite in metamorphic rocks characteristically yields:

options.b: Pinite (fine-grained aggregate of muscovite/sericite and chlorite)

notes: Pinite is a green to yellowish-brown microcrystalline pseudomorph after cordierite composed of fine-grained white mica (sericite) and chlorite.

question: Which of the following highly disharmonic, tortuous micro-folds are commonly associated with migmatites and high-grade anatectic gneisses?
notes: Ptygmatic folds are highly tortuous, meandering pegmatitic/granitic leucosome veins buckled within ductile, plastically deforming migmatite paleosomes.

question: In the triangular ACF compatibility diagrams (Eskola, 1915) used to represent metamorphic facies assemblages, the apex 'A' is calculated as:
notes: In Eskola's ACF diagram: A = Al2O3 + Fe2O3 - (Na2O + K2O); C = CaO - 3.3 P2O5; F = FeO + MgO + MnO, correcting for alkalis tied up in feldspars.

question: The process of complete ultra-metamorphic remelting of crustal rocks with the generation of new granitic magma is termed:
notes: Anatexis refers to the partial to complete melting of pre-existing rocks under high-grade metamorphism, generating granitic migmatites and neomagmas (palingenesis).

question: Under water-saturated crustal conditions (PH2O = Ptotal ~ 3-5 kbar), anatectic melting (palingenesis) of pelitic rocks initiates at approximately:
notes: Water-saturated minimum melting in the haplogranite system (Ab-Or-Qz-H2O) begins at ~650°C at 5 kbar, marking the transition from granulites to anatexis.

question: Which of the following is NOT an effect of alkali metasomatism?

options.d: Replacement of hornblende by biotite in the granitization of amphibolite

notes: Greisenization is an acid-fluorine pneumatolytic/hydrothermal alteration that strips alkalis (converting feldspars to quartz + topaz + white mica), rather than alkali addition.

question: Tourmalinization in granitic aureoles and pegmatites is the metasomatic result of the introduction of:
notes: Tourmalinization occurs when volatile boron- and fluorine-rich hydrothermal fluids from cooling granites metasomatize wall-rock aluminosilicates into tourmaline.

question: When quartzo-feldspathic rocks undergo dynamothermal alteration wherein alkali feldspars break down into fine white mica (sericite) and quartz, the process is termed:
notes: Sericitization is the hydrothermal/metamorphic alteration of K-feldspar or plagioclase into fine-grained white mica (sericite) plus quartz under acidic hydrous conditions.

question: Which of the following metamorphic rocks is essentially composed of hornblende and calcic plagioclase (labradorite/andesine) with little to no quartz?
notes: An amphibolite is a basic metamorphic rock composed of roughly equal proportions of green/brown hornblende and plagioclase, formed in the amphibolite facies.

question: When pelitic shales are subjected to high-temperature contact metamorphism against a granitic intrusion, the characteristic rock formed is a:
notes: Shales undergo desiccation and solid-state recrystallization in the inner contact aureole, producing tough, non-foliated, fine-grained hornfelses.

question: Contact metamorphism of an impure dolomitic limestone with both alumina and silica impurities leads to the crystallization of:
notes: With both Al2O3 and SiO2 present in a dolomitic host, high-temperature thermal decarbonation yields Mg-silicates (forsterite) and Mg-Al oxides (spinel, MgAl2O4).

question: 'Leptynite' (or leptite) is petrographically defined as a:

options.a: Fine-grained acidic meta-igneous rock with a granulose structure
options.b: Granulite-facies garnetiferous quartzofeldspathic gneiss with granoblastic structure

notes: In Indian Precambrian petrology, leptynites are quartzofeldspathic granulites containing almandine-pyrope garnet, quartz, and microperthite with granulose texture.

question: Choose the correct sequence of progressive mechanical deformation of hard, brittle rocks under increasing cataclastic strain along a fault zone:

options.a: Augen structure -> Mortar structure -> Flaser rock -> Mylonite
options.b: Mortar structure -> Augen structure -> Flaser rock -> Cataclasite -> Mylonite
options.c: Cataclasite -> Mortar structure -> Flaser rock -> Mylonite
options.d: Flaser rock -> Mortar structure -> Cataclasite -> Mylonite

notes: Progressive cataclastic deformation initiates with marginal grain crushing (mortar), develops augen porphyroclasts, produces shear lenses (flasers), and culminates in mylonitization.

question: Which of the following metamorphic rocks does NOT exhibit an equigranular granulose/granoblastic structure?
notes: Adinoles, marbles, and skarns are typically granulose/granoblastic, whereas Khondalites are distinctly foliated and banded gneisses.

question: The critical mineralogy of which contact metamorphic facies is thermodynamically similar to that of the medium-grade regional amphibolite facies?
notes: The hornblende-hornfels facies forms at temperatures equivalent to the regional amphibolite facies (~500-650°C), crystallizing hornblende + plagioclase in basic rocks.

question: The critical mineralogy of the contact pyroxene-hornfels facies corresponds thermodynamically to which regional metamorphic facies?
notes: Both pyroxene-hornfels and regional granulite facies represent anhydrous high temperatures (>650-800°C) with orthopyroxene + clinopyroxene + plagioclase assemblages.

question: The mineral assemblage Albite + Epidote + Actinolite + Chlorite + Quartz is uniquely diagnostic of which regional metamorphic facies?
notes: Greenschist facies metabasites are characterized by albite + epidote + actinolite + chlorite (giving the rock its green color), formed at 300-450°C.

question: In the metamorphic petrology of basic volcanic rocks, the transition from Greenschist facies to Amphibolite facies is marked by:

options.b: Change from albite (<An10) to calcic plagioclase (>An15-20) and actinolite to hornblende

notes: The peristerite gap transition marks the boundary: sodic albite jumps to oligoclase/andesine, while pale actinolite recrystallizes into aluminous hornblende.

question: The diagnostic mineral assemblage of an unretrograded Eclogite facies metabasite consists of:
notes: True eclogites are bimineralic rocks consisting of green omphacite pyroxene and red pyrope-almandine garnet, completely lacking plagioclase feldspar.

question: Which of the following minerals is the definitive diagnostic index mineral for the Granulite facies in both basic and intermediate rocks?
notes: The appearance of orthopyroxene (hypersthene/enstatite) through dehydration of amphibole defines the entry into the granulite facies.

question: The low-grade metamorphic facies characterized by prehnite, pumpellyite, albite, and quartz (200-300°C) is the:
notes: The prehnite-pumpellyite facies bridges the gap between zeolite and greenschist facies, characterized by prehnite + pumpellyite in altered basaltic rocks.

question: The lowest grade of regional metamorphism characterized by zeolites (laumontite, wairakite) replacing volcanic glass and plagioclase is the:
notes: The zeolite facies (100-200°C, low P) marks the onset of burial metamorphism in thick volcanic/volcaniclastic basins.

question: In George Barrow's (1893) classic metamorphic zones of the Scottish Dalradian Highlands, the lowest temperature index zone is the:
notes: The chlorite zone marks the lowest grade of Barrovian pelitic metamorphism (upper greenschist conditions), with fine-grained chlorite and white mica.

question: In Barrovian metamorphic zonation, the 'Biotite isograd' represents the first appearance of brown biotite formed through the reaction between:
notes: Biotite forms at ~400-450°C via the reaction: Chlorite + Muscovite -> Biotite + more aluminous Chlorite + Quartz + H2O.

question: In Barrovian regional metamorphism of pelites, the 'Garnet zone' is characterized by the first appearance of idioblastic crystals of:
notes: The Barrovian garnet isograd marks the entry of almandine-rich garnet formed by reaction of chlorite + quartz at ~500°C.

question: The Staurolite zone in Barrovian pelitic sequences is characteristic of which metamorphic grade?
notes: Staurolite appears in the lower amphibolite facies via the breakdown of chloritoid or chlorite + muscovite, serving as a classic medium-grade Barrovian marker.

question: A line on a geological map joining points of equal metamorphic grade, defined by the first appearance of a diagnostic index mineral, is termed an:
notes: C.E. Tilley (1924) introduced the term 'isograd' to represent lines on a map connecting points where a specific metamorphic reaction first occurred.

question: The correct progressive Barrovian sequence of index zones in pelitic rocks from lowest to highest grade is:

options.a: Chlorite -> Garnet -> Biotite -> Staurolite -> Kyanite -> Sillimanite
options.b: Biotite -> Chlorite -> Garnet -> Kyanite -> Staurolite -> Sillimanite
options.c: Chlorite -> Biotite -> Garnet -> Staurolite -> Kyanite -> Sillimanite
options.d: Sillimanite -> Kyanite -> Staurolite -> Garnet -> Biotite -> Chlorite

notes: Barrow's classic Barrovian sequence in pelites is: Chlorite -> Biotite -> Almandine Garnet -> Staurolite -> Kyanite -> Sillimanite.

question: In Buchan (Abukuma) low-pressure regional metamorphic terranes, which index minerals replace kyanite and staurolite in pelitic sequences?
notes: In low-pressure Buchan-type belts (high geothermal gradient), the low-density polymorph andalusite and cordierite crystallize instead of high-pressure kyanite and staurolite.

question: Akiho Miyashiro's (1961) classic concept of 'Paired Metamorphic Belts' describes the parallel juxtaposition along convergent plate margins of:

options.a: A high-P/T belt (subduction trench side) and a low-P/T belt (magmatic arc side)
options.c: A granulite belt and a zeolite belt

notes: Paired metamorphic belts reflect subduction zone geometry: cold oceanic subduction produces an outer high P/T blueschist belt, while arc magmatism produces an inner low P/T belt.

question: A 'Skarn' (tactite) is an allochemical metamorphic rock produced by calc-silicate metasomatism, composed predominantly of:

options.c: Grossular/andradite garnet, diopside/hedenbergite, wollastonite, and epidote

notes: Skarns form at igneous-carbonate contacts through silica/iron infiltration, crystallizing calc-silicate assemblages (grossular-andradite, diopside, wollastonite, epidote).

question: 'Fenitization' is a high-temperature alkaline metasomatic process associated characteristically with the intrusion of:
notes: Fenitization produces aureoles (fenites) rich in aegirine, sodic amphibole (arfvedsonite), and alkali feldspar around carbonatite and nepheline syenite complexes.

question: The hydrothermal alteration of calcic plagioclase into an intimate fine-grained aggregate of zoisite/epidote, albite, calcite, and sericite is termed:
notes: Saussuritization is the retrograde breakdown of calcic plagioclase in altered gabbros/dolerites into a dense greenish aggregate of epidote/zoisite + albite.

question: The pseudomorphic replacement of primary pyroxenes (augite) by fibrous or prismatic secondary amphibole (actinolite/hornblende) is termed:
notes: Uralitization is the deuteric or low-grade metamorphic alteration of pyroxene into secondary fibrous amphibole (uralite) without destruction of the original crystal outline.

question: The hydration of ultramafic forsteritic olivine and pyroxene in peridotites by aqueous fluids at temperatures < 400°C produces:
notes: Serpentinization hydrologically alters mantle peridotites into serpentine minerals [Mg3Si2O5(OH)4] plus magnetite and brucite with substantial volume expansion.

question: The Charnockite Series (Sir Thomas Holland, 1900) of Southern India is petrologically characterized by the ubiquitous presence of:

options.a: Orthopyroxene (Hypersthene) with distinctive pleochroism in all members from acid to ultrabasic

notes: Thomas Holland (1900) established the Charnockite series based on the St. Thomas Mount rock in Madras, defined by orthopyroxene (hypersthene) across the entire suite.

question: 'Gondite' (Sir L.L. Fermor, 1909) is a metamorphosed manganiferous sedimentary rock composed essentially of:
notes: Fermor (1909) named the Gondite series from the Gond tribe of Central India for non-calcareous manganiferous arenaceous sediments metamorphosed to spessartine + quartz.

question: 'Kodurite' (Fermor, 1909) of Andhra Pradesh is a manganiferous rock suite composed essentially of:
notes: Kodurite represents an igneous/hybrid suite of K-feldspar + Mn-garnet (spessartine-andradite) + apatite, associated with the manganese deposits of Kodur, AP.

question: 'Khondalite' (T.L. Walker, 1902) of the Eastern Ghats is scientifically defined as a:
notes: Named by T.L. Walker (1902) after the Khond hill tribes of Kalahandi, Orissa, Khondalites are aluminous metapelitic granulites composed of quartz + garnet + sillimanite + graphite.

question: In Ultra-High-Pressure (UHP) metamorphic rocks, the presence of which silica polymorph provides definitive evidence for pressures exceeding 28 kbar (~90 km mantle depth)?
notes: Chopin (1984) discovered coesite inclusions preserved inside pyrope megacrysts in the Dora-Maira massif, proving continental crust subduction to depths >90 km.

question: Microdiamonds preserved as inclusions within metamorphic garnets and zircons indicate subduction of continental crust to minimum depths of:
notes: Metamorphic diamond (e.g., Kokchetav Massif, Kazakhstan) requires minimum pressures of 4 GPa (~40 kbar), demonstrating crustal descent to >120-140 km before exhumation.

question: The mineral assemblage characteristic of basic rocks in the glaucophane-schist (blueschist) facies is:

options.d: Glaucophane + Lawsonite / Epidote + Jadeitic Pyroxene + Quartz

notes: Metabasites in the blueschist facies are characterized by the diagnostic high P/T minerals glaucophane + lawsonite + aragonite + jadeite.

question: The decomposition of muscovite in the presence of quartz at high metamorphic temperatures marks the 'second sillimanite isograd', represented by the reaction:
notes: At ~650-700°C, the breakdown of muscovite + quartz eliminates primary muscovite and generates K-feldspar + sillimanite + water, defining the upper amphibolite boundary.

question: Which of the following metamorphic reactions represents a discontinuous decarbonation reaction in siliceous limestones?
notes: The classic reaction: CaCO3 (Calcite) + SiO2 (Quartz) -> CaSiO3 (Wollastonite) + CO2 occurs at ~600°C in contact skarns with continuous CO2 expulsion.

question: In metamorphic petrology, 'Anatexis' is defined as:

options.a: Brittle crushing of rocks during faulting
options.b: The partial melting of pre-existing crustal rocks under extreme thermal metamorphism

notes: Anatexis is the differential melting of rocks in high-grade metamorphic belts, producing migmatitic leucosomes and granitic melts.

question: In a migmatite complex, the dark, residual, unmelted refractory part enriched in biotite, cordierite, or sillimanite is termed the:
notes: K.R. Mehnert (1968) divided migmatites into: Leucosome (light quartzofeldspathic melt), Melanosome (dark restite residue), Neosome (newly formed part), and Paleosome (unaltered host).

question: In migmatite terminology, the light-colored, quartz- and feldspar-rich granitic fraction that crystallized from the in-situ partial melt is the:
notes: The leucosome represents the crystallized granitic/pegmatitic melt fraction generated by anatexis in migmatites.

question: Which of the following metamorphic mineral textures is characterized by the vermicular, graphic, or worm-like intergrowth of two minerals formed during retrograde or decompression breakdown?
notes: Symplectites are fine-grained, vermicular intergrowths (e.g., clinopyroxene + spinel after omphacite, or biotite + quartz) formed during rapid decompression or retrograde breakdown.

question: A reaction rim or halo of secondary minerals completely surrounding a central reactant mineral grain is termed a:
notes: Coronas form by diffusion-controlled solid-state reaction between incompatible adjacent minerals (e.g., orthopyroxene-clinopyroxene-spinel halos around olivine next to plagioclase).

question: Which of the following minerals is strictly an 'anti-stress' mineral, whose crystallization is favored in static thermal environments and suppressed by directed shear stress?
notes: Cordierite and andalusite have low densities, large open ring/cage lattice structures, and large molar volumes, making them typical anti-stress minerals of static contact aureoles.

question: The polymorph of Al2SiO5 that possesses the lowest specific gravity (~3.15 g/cm3) and is characteristic of low-pressure contact aureoles and Buchan belts is:
notes: Andalusite (orthorhombic, density ~3.15 g/cm3) is the stable Al2SiO5 phase at low pressures (<3.8 kbar) in contact hornfelses and low P/T regional belts.

question: The fibrous, needle-like variety of sillimanite common in high-grade pelitic schists and gneisses is termed:
notes: Fibrolite consists of fine, felted mats of microscopic sillimanite needles, commonly nucleating on biotite at the entry to the sillimanite zone.

question: The variety of andalusite that displays a cross-like black cross of carbonaceous and clay inclusions along crystallographic axes is termed:
notes: Chiastolite displays a distinctive black cross formed by selective adsorption of graphite/clay impurities along prism edges during porphyroblastic growth in carbonaceous slates.

question: In the contact metamorphism of pure limestone (CaCO3), calcite recrystallizes into a coarse interlocking granoblastic mosaic producing:
notes: In pure limestone, no chemical reaction occurs; solid-state recrystallization of calcite grains minimizes surface free energy, producing granoblastic polygonal calcite marble.

question: The presence of hydrous low-temperature minerals like chlorite, actinolite, epidote, and albite is characteristic of the:
notes: Abundant structural (OH)-bearing phyllosilicates and inosilicates (chlorite, actinolite, epidote) define the hydrous low-temperature greenschist facies.

question: The decarbonation reaction: CaMgSi2O6 (Diopside) + Mg2SiO4 (Forsterite) + 2 CaCO3 (Calcite) -> 3 X + 2 CO2 marks the transition to extreme contact conditions. The mineral X is:
notes: Monticellite (CaMgSiO4) forms at high temperatures by reaction of diopside, forsterite, and calcite with CO2 expulsion: Di + Fo + 2 Cal -> 3 Monticellite + 2 CO2.

question: The transition boundary between burial diagenesis and the zeolite metamorphic facies in volcaniclastic basins is marked by the appearance of:
notes: The transformation of smectite/glass to heulandite and laumontite marks the formal entry into the zeolite facies at temperatures of ~100-150°C.

question: The mineral pumpellyite, diagnostic of the Prehnite-Pumpellyite facies, is structurally a:

options.c: Hydrous Ca-Al-Mg sorosilicate related to epidote

notes: Pumpellyite [Ca2MgAl2(SiO4)(Si2O7)(OH)2·H2O] is a complex hydrous sorosilicate containing both isolated SiO4 and paired Si2O7 groups, related structurally to epidote.

question: Regional metamorphic rocks of the classic Greenschist facies develop along which type of geothermal gradient?

options.a: Normal to moderate continental geothermal gradient (~20-35°C/km)

notes: Greenschist facies rocks develop under standard orogenic geothermal gradients (20-35°C/km) in medium P/T Barrovian collisional belts.

question: Which of the following calcium silicate minerals is thermodynamically stable exclusively at LOW lithostatic pressures and elevated temperatures in contact aureoles?
notes: Wollastonite (CaSiO3) formation from Calcite + Quartz is favored by low total pressure and low CO2 partial pressure, characteristic of contact metamorphic skarns.

question: The Fe2+/Mg exchange distribution coefficient between coexisting orthopyroxene and clinopyroxene: KD = (Fe2+/Mg)opx / (Fe2+/Mg)cpx serves as a geothermometer. In high-temperature igneous rocks KD is ~1.0-1.4, whereas in metamorphic granulites KD is approximately:
notes: The Wood-Banno two-pyroxene thermometer shows that KD increases as temperature drops: high-T igneous pyroxenes have KD ~1.1-1.3, whereas lower-temperature granulite pyroxenes have KD ~1.8-2.1.

question: In the high-grade crystalline basement of metamorphic terrains, eclogite lenses and tectonic pods occur commonly within:

options.c: Granulite facies migmatitic gneisses and subduction mélanges

notes: Eclogite relics survive as high-density retrogressed lenses and boudins enclosed within quartzofeldspathic granulites, amphibolites, and migmatites.

question: The primary diagnostic hydrous calcium-aluminum sorosilicate index mineral of the high-pressure blueschist facies is:
notes: Lawsonite is stable exclusively at high pressures (>3-4 kbar) and low temperatures (<400°C), breaking down to zoisite + kyanite + quartz at higher temperatures.

question: In the ultrabasic division of the Charnockite suite of rocks, the dominant mafic mineral is:
notes: Ultrabasic members of the charnockite suite are hypersthenites and pyroxenites composed almost entirely of orthopyroxene (hypersthene) ± clinopyroxene and olivine.

question: The mineral assemblage characteristic of pelitic rocks in the Greenschist facies is:
notes: In pelites, the greenschist facies is defined by fine-grained muscovite (sericite) + chlorite + quartz + albite.

question: Which of the following is the correct progressive sequence of George Barrow's (1893) classic index zones established in the Dalradian Highlands of Scotland?

options.a: Chlorite zone -> Biotite zone -> Garnet zone -> Staurolite zone -> Kyanite zone -> Sillimanite zone
options.b: Chlorite zone -> Garnet zone -> Biotite zone -> Staurolite zone -> Kyanite zone -> Sillimanite zone
options.c: Sillimanite zone -> Kyanite zone -> Staurolite zone -> Garnet zone -> Biotite zone -> Chlorite zone
options.d: Biotite zone -> Chlorite zone -> Garnet zone -> Staurolite zone -> Sillimanite zone -> Kyanite zone

notes: The Dalradian Highland sequence defines the global archetype for medium P/T Barrovian regional metamorphism.

question: Autometasomatic replacement of primary high-temperature silicates (feldspars, augite, olivine) by carbonates (calcite, dolomite, ankerite) in igneous rocks is termed:
notes: Carbonation is the introduction of CO2-rich fluids that convert Ca-Mg-Fe silicates into secondary carbonates (calcite, dolomite, ankerite) plus quartz.

question: The conversion of a hornblende-labradorite assemblage of an amphibolite into an albite-epidote-chlorite-calcite assemblage of a greenschist illustrates the process of:
notes: Reconstitution of a high-temperature amphibolite into low-temperature greenschist minerals with addition of H2O and CO2 is classic retrograde metamorphism.

question: Fixation of alkalis by ferromagnesian silicates, illustrated by the metasomatic replacement of hornblende by biotite during the granitization of amphibolite, is an example of:
notes: Infiltration of potassium-rich fluids converts calcic hornblende into potassic biotite: Hornblende + K+ -> Biotite + Ca2+.

question: Which of the following garnet species is the most common and widespread garnet found in regional metamorphic gneisses and mica schists?
notes: Almandine (the iron-aluminum garnet) is by far the most abundant garnet species in regional metapelitic schists, amphibolites, and gneisses.

question: Which of the following thermodynamic statements regarding the stability of plagioclase feldspar is true?

options.a: Plagioclase is stable at low temperatures and pressures
options.b: Plagioclase is stable at high temperatures and high pressures
options.c: Plagioclase is stable at high temperatures and moderate pressures, but becomes unstable at very high pressures (breaking down into jadeite/omphacite + garnet + quartz)
options.d: Plagioclase is stable at low temperatures but unstable at low pressures

notes: At pressures >12-15 kbar, plagioclase becomes thermodynamically unstable, breaking down via the reaction: Albite -> Jadeite + Quartz, and Anorthite -> Grossular + Kyanite + Quartz.

question: With the progressive increase in the grade of regional metamorphism in metabasites, the anorthite content (mole % An) of plagioclase feldspar:

options.a: Increases systematically (from Albite An0-5 in greenschists to Oligoclase An20 in amphibolites and Bytownite/Anorthite in granulites)
options.d: There is no relationship between anorthite content and metamorphic grade

notes: As metamorphic grade increases, Ca from epidote/calcite is progressively incorporated into plagioclase, driving its composition continuously from albite (An0-5) in greenschist facies to andesine/bytownite in granulites.
